definition: Parity is the state of being equal, especially in status, rights, level, or amount.

Similarity means two things are roughly alike, while parity means they stand at exactly the same level.
Parity makes two sides equal in level or amount, while uniformity makes everything identical in every respect.

Equality is the everyday, all-purpose word for being equal, at home anywhere from playgrounds to constitutions. Parity is its formal cousin: a measured state of equal level, status, or amount, used where the match can be checked — pay parity, prize-money parity. Kids demand equality; negotiators and policymakers pursue parity.

Equivalence means being the same in value or effect even when the forms differ — a bus transfer can stand in for a ticket. Parity is stricter: two sides at exactly the same level in the same terms, matched pay for matched work. Equivalence tolerates different forms of matching worth; parity demands the levels themselves match.

formal, technical register

Parity is a formal noun used where equality can be measured or compared directly, as in pay parity or parity in representation, and it often appears in the pattern 'parity between X and Y.' Parity measures equal levels between two things, unlike equitable, which judges whether an outcome is genuinely fair to people's different needs, or impartial, which describes an unbiased judge or process.

For forty years the tiny republic of Valdenne has pegged its franc to its neighbor's mark at strict parity: one franc equals one mark, today, tomorrow, always.
The peg makes life simple along the border.
Shopkeepers post a single price, workers compare wages across the river at a glance, and no one wastes a morning at the exchange window.
Keeping the promise is harder than making it.
When traders doubt the franc, the central bank must spend its reserves buying francs until the two currencies again trade one for one.
Twice the bank has nearly run dry defending the rate, and twice parliament has debated letting the franc float.
Both times the border towns objected loudest: their whole economy, they said, rests on knowing the two currencies are worth exactly the same.
